Kickapoo

Kickapoo people continue in distinct communities and governments across the United States and Mexico. This Texas-focused reading path concerns the Kickapoo Traditional Tribe of Texas and selected cross-border, legal, education, and housing sources; it does not represent every Kickapoo community.

Names & relationshipsKickapoo is a broad people-level directory entry spanning distinct communities and governments. This supplement focuses on the Kickapoo Traditional Tribe of Texas. It does not collapse the Texas, Oklahoma, Kansas, or Mexican communities into one government or imply that the Texas government represents all Kickapoo people.
A cited introduction, with more to explore.This overview draws together the linked sources below. It is an introduction, and does not replace community-authored histories or a full scholarly study.

The sources are relevant but uneven in perspective and do not yet provide a deep, community-authored history or a comprehensive account of all Kickapoo communities.

01

Distinct communities and the Texas-focused scope

Kickapoo people are represented by distinct communities and governments in the United States and Mexico. The 1983 Texas Band of Kickapoo Act used a specific legal relationship to the Kickapoo Tribe of Oklahoma; a later Interior Solicitor memorandum also describes the Texas Tribe as separate and apart in the context of a particular federal legal question. These sources document legal wording and chronology, not every community’s own account of identity.

Read the sources [3] U.S. Congress [4] U.S. Department of the Interior, Office of the Solicitor

02

Cross-border history and community participation

A 2020 scholarly article examines the effects of the U.S.–Mexico border on Kickapoo communities in Texas and Coahuila, drawing on earlier literature and interviews from 1985–2005. Its interpretations and interview accounts are tied to that author and period. A separate 2017 Texas intertribal public-safety report records the Texas Tribe’s participation in statewide planning; its schematic map serves the report’s planning purpose and does not define homelands.

Read the sources [5] Texas Tribal Strategic Advisory Group; Texas Department of Public Safety [6] Elisabeth Albine Mager Hois; Punto CUNorte

03

What the 1983 statute and 2020 legal memorandum address

The 1983 federal act authorizes specified services, land-acquisition activity in Maverick County, and border passage provisions. The 2020 Interior memorandum answers a narrower question about federal jurisdiction in 1934 and a particular fee-to-trust application, while discussing the later statute. Read together, they offer a bounded legal chronology. They do not establish current implementation or provide legal advice.

Read the sources [3] U.S. Congress [4] U.S. Department of the Interior, Office of the Solicitor

04

Education and language-related programs

The Texas Tribe’s education department describes its mission and lists education and language programs. The page labels some initiatives as under development. It is a brief statement of the department’s public-facing priorities; it does not establish which listed services are currently operating or their outcomes.

Read the sources [8] Kickapoo Traditional Tribe of Texas

05

A dated housing and community-development case study

A short HUD case feature describes housing and community-development projects involving the Texas Tribe, including FEMA mobile homes during 2009–2013 and a wellness-center project. The page’s publication date is unstated, so it is useful for a limited historical case study rather than present-day program or demographic information.

Read the sources [7] U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development

What needs further research

  • Seek substantive Texas Tribe-authored history and language/education publications beyond the brief department page.
  • Review the full 2025 TAMIU thesis; only its abstract and repository record were inspected.
  • Locate and read the Texas Tribe’s 1989 constitution and later primary legal/administrative records before describing present legal implementation.
  • Add distinct community perspectives from Kickapoo communities in Oklahoma, Kansas, and Mexico; the Texas supplement cannot stand for them.
  • The scholarly article draws on interviews from 1985–2005; current cross-border conditions remain unestablished.
  • No community review or endorsement is recorded.

Texas-focused supplement reviewed 2026-10-23. Five sources count toward the substantive target; the two existing homepages, brief Tribal education page, and unread-full-text TAMIU thesis are excluded. Legal sources are limited to their stated questions and dates. The 2017 report’s map is not reproduced or used as territorial evidence. No historical-map association was added in this source-focused batch.

GovernmentU.S. CongressSource 3

Texas Band of Kickapoo Act, Public Law 97-429 ↗

The 1983 statute names the Texas Band as a subgroup of the Kickapoo Tribe of Oklahoma, authorizes federal services and land acquisition in Maverick County, and addresses passage across the international border. It records the law as enacted then; it is not a complete account of later legal status or present implementation.

Inspection scope: Entire three-page enacted statute read; land authority, services and border-passage provisions inspected.

Content checked October 23, 2026

https://www.congress.gov/97/statute/STATUTE-96/STATUTE-96-Pg2269.pdf
Federal law·Texas·Border crossing
GovernmentU.S. Department of the Interior, Office of the SolicitorSource 4

Federal Jurisdiction Status of the Kickapoo Traditional Tribe of Texas in 1934 ↗

This 2020 solicitor memorandum addresses a specific federal-jurisdiction question and a pending fee-to-trust application. It distinguishes the 1934 Indian Reorganization Act analysis from the later 1983 statute. Its conclusion is limited to that legal issue and should not be read as a complete or current legal account, or as legal advice.

Inspection scope: PDF pages 1–7 and 23–24 inspected, including background and conclusion; the other pages and current implementation were not reviewed.

Content checked October 23, 2026

Government / intertribal reportTexas Tribal Strategic Advisory Group; Texas Department of Public SafetySource 5

Tribes of Texas Report ↗

A 2017 public-safety broadband report includes a Kickapoo Traditional Tribe of Texas profile and documents the Tribe’s participation in a statewide intertribal planning effort. The migration map is schematic and designed for this report’s purpose; it is not reproduced or treated as a homeland boundary. Dated population and service figures are excluded.

Inspection scope: Inspected PDF pages 4–5, 12–13 and 19–21, including participant list, map context and Kickapoo profile; references screened. Other profiles and dated population/service figures not used.

Academic / referenceElisabeth Albine Mager Hois; Punto CUNorteSource 6

El problema de la frontera México-Estados Unidos para la tribu kikapu de Coahuila-Texas ↗

This Spanish-language scholarly article analyzes how the U.S.–Mexico border affected Kickapoo communities in Texas and Coahuila. It combines earlier published literature with interviews conducted between 1985 and 2005. Interpretations and interview accounts are attributed to the author and their stated period; disagreements and broad claims are not presented as settled facts.

Inspection scope: Full article body, from abstract and introduction through relevant historical sections, conclusion and references, read. Restricted cultural descriptions were deliberately excluded from the synthesis.

Content checked October 23, 2026
